structure.title: Two bargains
structure.text: A loan in Venice and a courtship test in Belmont establish parallel questions about promises, money, and judgment.

structure.title: Claims tested
structure.text: The plots converge as obligations are enforced and interpreted. Comic exchanges continue to test the meanings of keeping one's word.

context.title: Religious hostility
context.text: Anti-Jewish prejudice shapes social and legal relationships in the play. Shylock's conduct occurs within that hostility without becoming exempt from judgment.

context.title: Choice under conditions
context.text: Both lending and courtship are constrained by prior rules. The appearance of free agreement can conceal pressure.
context.takeaway: Ask who can set or reinterpret the terms.

notice.text: Compare speeches about mercy with actual treatment.
notice.why: A proclaimed virtue can be unevenly distributed.
Objects give invisible obligations a visible form.

opening: Bassanio needs money to court a wealthy woman, and his friend Antonio is willing to borrow it for him. The lender, Shylock, belongs to a community Antonio despises, and proposes a penalty that sounds too grotesque to become real. Shakespeare sets the bargain beside a romantic contest in which another person's fortune is also at stake. Promises, prejudice, and calculated generosity draw the stories together, until the people most fluent in the language of mercy have to demonstrate what they mean by it.
